title: Isaiah 44:28-45:1 (Cyrus the shepherd and anointed)
venue: Sefaria (JPS 1985 and Miqra according to the Masorah)
ask_addressed: Quote the biblical and Persian texts that bear on Persian-Judaean contact
quote: He shall say of Jerusalem, ‘She shall be rebuilt,’
summary: A prophetic oracle names the Persian king Cyrus as God's 'anointed' (mashiach) and as the one who will say Jerusalem 'shall be rebuilt' and the temple 'founded again'. It shows a Judaean text welcoming Persian rule; it does not show any Persian knowledge of Judah.
limits: Hebrew 'meshiho' is rendered 'the anointed one' by JPS. Dating of the oracle to before 539 is the consensus view; a post-539 date is argued by some. The passage does not demonstrate a Persian policy toward Judaeans, and says nothing about Zoroastrian ideas.

text.edition: Sefaria API: JPS Tanakh 1985 gender-sensitive (English), Miqra according to the Masorah (Hebrew)

composition.basis: Chs 40-55 are widely dated to the Exile, 6th c. BCE ('an anonymous author writing during the Exile in the 6th century BCE'), per the Wikipedia article 'Book of Isaiah' (opened 2026-11-17); a tertiary summary, not the scholars it cites.

text.witness: Great Isaiah Scroll 1QIsa-a, Qumran Cave 1: calibrated radiocarbon range 356-103 BCE, palaeographic 150-100 BCE (Wikipedia 'Isaiah Scroll', citing Jull et al. 1995; not independently opened). Masoretic witnesses are far later and were not checked.

title: Isaiah 45:5-7 ('I form light and create darkness')
venue: Sefaria (JPS 1985 and Miqra according to the Masorah)
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open
quote: I form light and create darkness
summary: Addressed to Cyrus, the verse asserts one God as maker of both light and darkness, weal and woe. It is often read as an answer to a Persian two-principle outlook, but the text itself names no Persian doctrine.
limits: Whether Isa 45:7 is aimed at Zoroastrian dualism is disputed; the ISBE entry opened here says there is 'almost certainly no reference to Mazdean dualism' in it. The passage alone shows monotheistic polemic, not borrowing.

title: Ezra 1:1-4 (Edict of Cyrus, Hebrew version)
venue: Sefaria (JPS 1985 and Miqra according to the Masorah)

quote: God of Heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth and has charged me with building a house
summary: Cyrus is reported to proclaim, in Hebrew, that the God of Heaven charged him to build a house in Jerusalem and to let people go up; neighbours are to help with silver, gold and goods.
limits: The wording is Judaean, not a Persian chancery text, and the Cyrus Cylinder (opened) does not mention Jerusalem or Judah. Authenticity of this proclamation is debated; the Aramaic version at Ezra 6:3-5 differs in form.

title: Ezra 6:3-5 (memorandum of Cyrus, Aramaic section)
venue: Sefaria (JPS 1985 and Miqra according to the Masorah)
ask_addressed: Quote the biblical and Persian texts that bear on Persian-Judaean contact
quote: Let the house be rebuilt, a place for offering sacrifices
summary: In the Aramaic section a record of Cyrus's first year orders the house of God rebuilt at royal expense, with set dimensions, and the temple vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar returned.
limits: This is a document quoted inside a narrative composed centuries later; its authenticity is argued both ways. Ezra 1 and 6 give different forms of the same decision (proclamation versus archive memorandum). Aramaic was the Persian empire's chancery language, which supports a documentary setting but does not prove it.

title: Esther 1:13-15 (Persian court procedure: dat, the seven princes)
venue: Sefaria (JPS 1985 and Miqra according to the Masorah)
ask_addressed: Quote the biblical and Persian texts that bear on Persian-Judaean contact
quote: the seven ministers of Persia and Media who had access to the royal presence
summary: The Hebrew uses Persian court vocabulary: 'dat' (law, from Old Persian) in 'yode'ei dat vadin', 'partemim' (nobles) at 1:3, and Ahasuerus (from Xshayarsha). The scene is a council of seven.

The Persian etymologies are stated from general knowledge of the Hebrew; this run opened the Hebrew text but no lexicon. Wikipedia 'Book of Esther' (opened) notes Ahasuerus derives from Xshayarsha and that the author 'displays an accurate knowledge of Persian customs and palaces'. The Qumran caves have produced no Esther fragment (Wikipedia 'Dead Sea Scrolls').

title: Daniel 6:1-10 and 6:11-17 (law of the Medes and Persians)
venue: Sefaria (JPS 1985 and Miqra according to the Masorah)

summary: Darius the Mede appoints 120 satraps and three ministers; an irrevocable ban on petitioning anyone but the king sends Daniel to the lions' den.
limits: Chapter 6 is a court tale; 'Darius the Mede' is not otherwise known as a king, and the Hebrew Bible dating of Daniel (167-163 BCE for the whole book per Wikipedia) postdates Persian rule. 'Satrap' is a Persian title; the passage shows later memory of Persian administration.

title: Daniel 12:1-3 (Michael, resurrection, judgement)
venue: Sefaria (JPS 1985 and Miqra according to the Masorah)
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open
quote: Many of those that sleep in the dust of the earth will awake
summary: The angel Michael appears at a time of trouble, and the dead awake, some to eternal life and some to everlasting abhorrence. This is the earliest undisputed Hebrew Bible statement of resurrection and the focus of the question whether Persian eschatology shaped it.

title: Cyrus Cylinder (translation, Livius, after Cogan and Schaudig), lines 12-15
ask_addressed: Quote the biblical and Persian texts that bear on Persian-Judaean contact
quote: he took a righteous king, his favorite, by the hand, he called out his name
summary: Marduk searches all lands, takes Cyrus by the hand and names him, and leads him to Babylon 'like a companion and a friend'. The language of being taken by the hand and named parallels Isaiah 45:1,4, but the god is Marduk.
limits: The parallel is formal: both are Near Eastern royal-appointment topoi. Neither text cites the other; no route is documented. Translation is Livius's adaptation of Cogan (Context of Scripture) and Schaudig, not the original Akkadian.

ask_addressed: Quote the biblical and Persian texts that bear on Persian-Judaean contact

title: Yasna 30.3-6 (the two primal Spirits), Mills translation
authors: Mills, L. H. (translator); Peterson, J. H. (digital edition)
ask_addressed: the Gathas (Yasna 30) and the Avestan material on angels and a final judgement, only as far as you can read an edition
quote: Now the two primal Spirits, who reveal themselves in vision as Twins, are the Better and the Bad
summary: The Gatha states a choice between two primal spirits, 'the Better and the Bad', who created 'Life and Not-Life'; the Daevas chose wrongly. Boyce's modern translation of the same verses (Livius) says 'there are two primal Spirits, twins renowned to be in conflict'.
limits: Mills (1898) is an old translation; Boyce's differs in detail (Livius, opened). The dating of the Gathas is unresolved (see text.composition) and may precede or follow the Babylonian exile. The text shows an ethical dualism of choice; whether it is the same as later Zoroastrian cosmic dualism is itself contested. No source opened shows Judaeans reading it.

text.witness: Oldest surviving Avestan manuscript 1288 CE, all extant manuscripts derive from a 9th-10th c. CE copy (Bremmer, as reported by Ehrman blog, opened); no ancient manuscripts.

title: Yasna 30.7-10 (retribution, the Consummation, molten metal), Mills translation
authors: Mills, L. H. (translator); Peterson, J. H. (digital edition)
ask_addressed: the Gathas (Yasna 30) and the Avestan material on angels and a final judgement, only as far as you can read an edition
quote: So when there cometh their punishment for their sins, then, O Mazda, at Thy command shall Good Thought establish the Dominion in the Consummation
summary: Verses 7-10 speak of punishment for the followers of the Lie, a Dominion established 'in the Consummation', retribution 'through (molten) metal', and a reward in the abode of Good Thought. This is the Gathic material nearest a final reckoning.
limits: Mills's wording differs from Boyce's, who has 'Then when retribution comes for these sinners ... may we be those who shall transfigure this world' (Livius). The Gatha has no clear individual resurrection; later Zoroastrian eschatology (Frashokereti, Saoshyant) is in the Younger Avesta and Pahlavi books, not in this passage. Verse 8 is not a proof of influence on Daniel 12.

authors: Mills, L. H. (translator); Peterson, J. H. (digital edition)

quote: I will bring his soul over the Bridge of Chinvat, I who am Ahura Mazda
summary: In a Younger Avestan chapter on the Ahuna-vairya prayer, Ahura Mazda promises to bring the reciter's soul over the Chinvat Bridge to heaven. It is Avestan evidence for a post-mortem crossing and a best-world destination.

This is Younger Avestan, later than the Gathas, with no firm date. Bremmer (via Ehrman) says the oldest Avestan texts give only one reference to a later life and none to a future judgement day.

title: Zoroastrianism (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, section on relation to Israel)
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open
quote: there is nothing in the formal theology of Judaism that can be described as "borrowed" from Mazdean teachings
summary: The entry lists what appears after Persian contact (angelology, a Satan figure, eschatology) but concludes the most that can be asserted is a mark on angelology and demonology and 'possibly' some eschatological details; Isa 45:7 'almost certainly' does not refer to Mazdean dualism.
limits: Early-20th-century reference work; unsigned on the page and the author is not shown; the Pahlavi and Avesta dating it assumes is outdated. It also grants influence on angelology and on 'common people'. Position is a cautious sceptic, not a denial.

title: Was Resurrection a Zoroastrian Idea? (Ehrman, quoting Bremmer 2002)
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open
quote: There … is little reason to derive Jewish ideas about resurrection from Persian sources. Their origin(s) may well lie in intra-Jewish developments
summary: Ehrman reports that Bremmer (The Rise and Fall of the Afterlife, 2002, p. 59) rejects a Persian origin for Jewish resurrection belief, noting the oldest Avestan manuscript is from 1288 CE and that resurrection appears in Jewish texts only from the Maccabean period, about 150 years after Persian rule.
limits: A blog post whose first part is public; the argument is secondhand from Bremmer, whose book I did not open. Ehrman says he will read Barr's 1985 JAAR article and had not yet reached a final view. The chronological argument concerns resurrection only, not angelology or dualism.

title: Views of Scholars Refuting Zoroastrian Influence (Antia, quoting Mark S. Smith)
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open
quote: "This dualism," he observes, "does not truly resemble biblical monotheism."
summary: Antia's compilation quotes Mark S. Smith (The Origins of Biblical Monotheism, OUP 2001) as doubting that Zoroastrianism was the model for biblical monotheism, while allowing that Persian tradition may have 'reinforced monotheistic rhetoric'. Antia disputes parts of Smith's reading.
limits: Partisan compilation by a Zoroastrian-community writer (Antia, January 2012); the Smith quote is secondhand and I did not open Smith's book. Smith concedes some Persian reinforcement. Included as a located statement of the sceptical case, not as proof.

title: Iranian influence on Judaism (Silverman, The Bible and Interpretation)
venue: The Bible and Interpretation (Arizona Center for Judaic Studies)
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open
quote: The entire area of Iranian influence has been beset by severe problems in method.
summary: Silverman, who argues for Iranian influence, states that earlier work was marred by racist assumptions and by failing to define 'influence', transmission or context, and says no earlier effort was 'wholly successful'. He argues for a borrowing in Daniel's metal-statue vision.
limits: Author is a proponent (Persepolis and Jerusalem, T&T Clark 2012), so this is a methodological caution from inside the camp, not a sceptic's rebuttal. Web article, Oct. 2011.

title: Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), dating
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open

summary: 1QIsa-a, the Great Isaiah Scroll, has been dated by radiocarbon to a calibrated 356-103 BCE and by palaeography to about 150-100 BCE; it is the earliest complete Isaiah witness and contains chs 44-45.
limits: Wikipedia summary citing Jull et al. (Radiocarbon 37, 1995); I did not open Jull et al. The Cyrus oracle's composition is much earlier than this copy, so the scroll fixes a latest date only.

title: Book of Daniel: Qumran manuscripts and dating
ask_addressed: Give composition ranges with their basis, the earliest witnesses, and the scholarly debate on how far Zoroastrian ideas shaped Judaism; quote the strongest sceptical scholar you can open
quote: All eight manuscripts were copied between 125 BC
summary: Eight Daniel copies from Qumran range from 125 BCE (4QDan-c) to about 50 CE, and the scholarly consensus dates the book to 167-163 BCE, so the earliest witness is within decades of composition.
limits: Wikipedia, tertiary; its citations (VanderKam and Flint; Collins) were not opened. The late date is what makes Persian-period borrowing hard to document.
